opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it really comes down to the nature of the two problems and the data we have for each. Locomotion is a very physical, very high-frequency control problem. You're running a policy at fifty, a hundred hertz or more, reacting to contacts, slips, disturbances, all within milliseconds. And what we've seen over the last few years is that reinforcement learning in simulation is extremely good at this. You can train in massively parallel simulation, thousands of robots at once, randomize the terrain, the dynamics, the sensor noise, and you get policies that transfer to the real robot and are remarkably robust. We basically have a recipe that works there.

Semantic planning is a completely different beast. It's about understanding the scene: what is this object, where should I go, what does the person want me to do. That's where the big vision-language models shine, because they've been trained on internet-scale data and they have this broad common-sense understanding. But those models are big, they're slow, they run at maybe one or a few hertz, and they don't really know anything about how to place a foot on a slippery step.

So if you try to merge everything into one end-to-end model right now, you run into problems on both sides. You don't have nearly enough real-world data that couples high-level semantics with low-level physical interaction to train that jointly. And simulation, which is what makes locomotion work, is not good at rendering realistic semantics, so you lose the strength of sim for the high-level part. You'd basically be making both problems harder at once.

Whereas if you separate them, with a clean interface in between, say velocity commands, waypoints, or target poses, each side can use the tool that works best for it. The locomotion policy becomes a reliable skill that you trust, almost like a primitive, and the high-level planner just has to tell it where to go. It's also much easier to debug: if something fails, you know whether the robot misunderstood the task or physically stumbled.

Long term, I do think these things will merge to some degree. There are cases where the high level really needs to know about physical capabilities, like whether the robot can actually climb that obstacle, and a fixed interface limits you there. But in the short term, given the data we have and how well each of these approaches works on its own, the modular approach is just the pragmatic way to get robots doing useful things in the real world.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the main reason is that the two problems live on completely different timescales and have completely different data requirements. Locomotion is fundamentally a high-frequency control problem. You're reacting to contacts, slips, terrain you can't see well, and you need decisions at hundreds of hertz. And the nice thing about that problem is that it's actually quite well defined. We know how to simulate it. We can generate essentially unlimited data in simulation, train a policy with reinforcement learning, and transfer it to the real robot. That recipe is pretty mature at this point. You can get a quadruped or a humanoid walking over stairs and rough terrain very robustly.

Semantic planning is a different beast. There you need to understand what an object is, what a human wants, what a kitchen is versus a hallway, and the knowledge you need comes from vision-language models and large pre-trained models that were built on internet-scale data. You can't simulate that. You can't train that from scratch with RL on a robot. And those models are slow, they reason at maybe a few hertz at best, and they're not precise enough to tell you where to put your foot.

So if you try to fold both into one end-to-end system today, you're asking a single network to be both a fast, reactive controller and a slow, knowledgeable reasoner, and you end up compromising on both. You lose the robustness of the low-level controller because now it's being trained on sparse, semantically labeled data, and you lose the generality of the planner because you're constraining it to the robot's specific morphology and sensors.

Whereas if you separate them, you get a very clean interface. The high-level system says "go there, follow that path, stand up, walk at this velocity," and the low-level policy handles the physics. You can swap either side independently. You can improve your foundation model without retraining the locomotion controller, and you can change the robot or improve the controller without touching the planner. That modularity is really valuable when both fields are moving as fast as they are.

I do think long term, the boundary will blur. There's clearly information the low-level controller would benefit from, like knowing that the surface ahead is ice or that the box is heavier than it looks, and that's semantic knowledge. So eventually you want tighter coupling, maybe a shared representation. But in the short term, given what works today, the decomposition is just the practical choice. It's the way to actually get robots out of the lab and doing useful things now rather than waiting for a fully unified model that we don't yet know how to train.

astra-6.text:
I think the main reason is that these two problems operate at very different levels. Locomotion is about reacting quickly to what’s happening physically: keeping your balance, making contact with the ground, and recovering when something doesn’t go as expected. Semantic planning is more about understanding what you want to accomplish and deciding which actions will get you there.

If you separate them, the planner can say, “Go over there,” and the locomotion controller can handle how to actually do that. You can train and test that controller on its own, and you don’t need to solve language understanding every time the robot takes a step.

An end-to-end approach could eventually be very powerful, because those levels do need to interact. But in the short term, it’s easier to make progress if we give each component a manageable problem and a clear interface. The important thing is that the planner gets feedback about what the robot can actually do, so it isn’t making plans that are physically impossible.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main reason is that these two problems operate at very different levels. For locomotion, you need a fast feedback loop. You need to react to what the robot is sensing, keep your balance, and adapt to the terrain. You don’t want that to depend on a semantic planner reasoning about the entire task.

At the higher level, you might say, “Go to the kitchen,” and the planner can figure out what that means and where the robot should go. Then a locomotion policy can handle how to actually get there, step by step. We have good tools for training those lower-level policies, particularly with reinforcement learning in simulation.

If you try to learn everything together, you’re asking one system to solve both the reasoning problem and the physical control problem, and getting the right training data and supervision becomes much harder. Separating them gives us something we can train, test, and improve independently. Long term, maybe that boundary becomes less explicit, but in the short term it seems like a much more practical way to build a capable robot.
